title: A year isn't 365 days. That's why Feb 29 exists 📅
description:
Why do we have leap years? A year isn't 365 days: Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours (365.2422 days) to go round the Sun. Ignore the extra hours and the calendar slips a day every 4 years, so Julius Caesar's calendar (45 BC) added February 29 every 4 years. But that's about 11 minutes a year too much, and by 1582 the seasons had drifted 10 days. Pope Gregory XIII's reform deleted them: Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October, and century years became leap years only if divisible by 400 (1900 wasn't, 2000 was). Without leap days, the seasons would flip in about 750 years.

Sources: OpenStax Astronomy 2e, 4.4 The Calendar; Britannica, The Gregorian calendar; Atlas Obscura, When the Pope made 10 days disappear.

meta.topic: why leap years exist: a year is ~365.2422 days (365 d + ~6 h); without the extra day the calendar slips 1 day every 4 years; Julian calendar (Caesar, 45 BC) adds Feb 29 every 4 years but is ~11 min/yr too long; by 1582 seasons drifted 10 days; Gregory XIII: 4 Oct 1582 -> 15 Oct; century rule (1900 no, 2000 yes); no leap days = seasons flip in ~750 years

scenes.say: You've been told a year is *365 days*. Wrong.
Earth needs *6 more hours* to lap the Sun.

scenes.say: Skip them, and every *4 years* you lose a *day*.

scenes.say: But Caesar's rule overshoots: *11 minutes* a year.
By *1582*, the seasons were *10 days* off.
So the Pope *deleted them*. October 4th, then *15th*.

scenes.say: That's why *1900* had no leap day. *2000* did.
Without it, in *750 years*, summer lands in *December*.
